papers.title: First documentation of Buprestis haemorrhoidalis (Coleoptera: Buprestidae) occurrence and damage in Korean wooden cultural heritage: population genetic structure and conservation implications
papers.abstract: Buprestis haemorrhoidalis Herbst, 1780 (Coleoptera: Buprestidae) is a Palaearctic wood-boring beetle associated with conifers and capable of developing in structural timber. Although this species is known to occur in Korea, its occurrence in wooden cultural heritage structures and its wood-boring activity have not previously been documented or investigated. We surveyed 58 sites in various regions of South Korea, including wooden cultural heritage sites, some designated as UNESCO World Heritage properties, and natural and timber-associated environments. We also examined mitochondrial genetic variation using maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis and haplotype networks based on cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) sequences from Korean specimens and reference sequences from Japan, the Russian Far East, and Europe. Adults were observed in natural and timber-associated environments, while adults and characteristic emergence holes were recorded at wooden cultural heritage sites, including the direct observation of an adult emerging from a wooden column. Analysis of 82 COI sequences identified 49 haplotypes and three mitochondrial subgroups (A-C). Subgroups A and B comprised predominantly Korean specimens and co-occurred at three sampling sites. Several haplotypes were shared among geographically separated Korean localities. This study provides the first documentation of B. haemorrhoidalis occurrence and associated evidence of wood-boring damage in Korean wooden cultural heritage, together with baseline information on its occurrence in human-made wooden environments and mitochondrial genetic variation. Shared COI haplotypes and historical timber-supply patterns raise the possibility of timber-mediated dispersal. These findings provide a foundation for monitoring this species and informing the conservation of wooden cultural heritage in Korea.

papers.title: Commentary on the nomenclatural status of Benthoctopus Grimpe, 1921 (Cephalopoda: Octopoda) and redescription of "Vulcanoctopus" pseudonymus (Grimpe, 1922)
papers.abstract: The nomenclatural status of the two octopus genera Bathypolypus Grimpe, 1921 and Benthoctopus Grimpe, 1921 has been the subject of considerable, at times contentious debate since both genera were first proposed. Of the two, Bathypolypus has nomenclatural priority, being the first mentioned of the two in Grimpe's cursory note. Although Benthoctopus was relegated to synonymy of Bathypolypus in 2002, the case for this synonymy was not compelling. The systematic complications generated by this act were subsequently aggravated by the description of another taxon, Muusoctopus Gleadall, 2004 (a replacement name proposed for taxa formerly attributed to Benthoctopus) and molecular data, that subsequently demonstrated Muusoctopus to be a junior synonym of Vulcanoctopus Gonzalez & Guerra, 1998. This created an untenable situation where multiple competing names were available to apply to many generally deep-dwelling octopus species with two rows of suckers, no ink sac, and either smooth or papillose bodies. Remnants of one important specimen historically attributed to the type species of the genus Benthoctopus (Be. piscatorum (Verrill, 1879)) are herein redescribed. Historical descriptions of this specimen are combined with modern observations and critically compared with what is reported for other North Atlantic Bathypolypus and Vulcanoctopus taxa to critique the original synonymy of Benthoctopus with Bathypolypus. The analysis demonstrates that the original synonymy of Benthoctopus with Bathypolypus cannot be upheld based on existing data, and the widespread nomenclatural repercussions of this status change are discussed. Finally, the type and only known specimen of Vulcanoctopus pseudonymus (Grimpe, 1922) comb. nov. is partly redescribed to facilitate a broader-scale revision of these problematic North Atlantic octopuses.

papers.title: Evaluation of window fullness at time of eclosion as an operational welfare indicator in farmed black soldier flies (Hermetia illucens)
papers.abstract: Body condition scoring can serve as an operational indicator of an animal's current welfare state and may also shed light on preceding, welfare-relevant conditions, such as stress. In farmed insects, limitations posed by the exoskeleton largely preclude traditional body condition assessment. However, adult black soldier flies (BSF) farmed in the insect protein industry have transparent abdominal panels that allow for visualisation of a portion of their fat body. Prior work has shown that the relative size of the fat body in the window, termed 'window fullness' (WF), at time of eclosion was reduced in adult females that were handled daily as prepupae (which also led to mortality, reduced body size, and developmental delays), suggesting it may predict prior stress. Accordingly, we investigated if WF correlated with relative lipid levels in newly emerged BSF; determined if assessors could score WF on an ordinal scale by eye; and assessed if WF changed when flies were pupated in non-preferred substrates. Relative lipid content strongly correlated with WF in males but not in females. Across all observers, WF could be scored by eye on an ordinal scale with 78.38% accuracy (range: 70.27 - 89.19%). Pupating in a preferred substrate correlated with increased dry mass and head widths for both sexes; females had increased WF (14.81%) but male WF was not affected. Overall, these data suggest WF could have promise as an on-farm-assessable indicator of body condition for BSF; however, there may be sex-specific differences in validity or reliability that require further investigation.

papers.title: Backstroke rowing as an adaptation for low-Reynolds-number flight in tiny whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci)
papers.abstract: The force resisting gravity during flight is typically aerodynamic-lift generated by the wings. However, in the smallest insects the low Reynolds number associated with a wing size [≤]1mm reduces the efficiency of using lift for flight. We examined how miniature whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) modulate their flapping kinematics to control flight in the vertical plane. Free-flying whiteflies were recorded using high-speed video cameras, and their 3D wing flapping kinematics were analyzed as a function of flight speed and climb angle. Whiteflies displayed the crescent-shaped wingtip trajectory typical to the drag-utilizing propulsion previously described in other miniature insects. To fly faster, they increased the wing sweep amplitude during the upstroke, resulting in increased wingtip speed relative to the body. To fly at steeper climbing angles the insects oriented their body to direct the upstroke wing motion downwards at a high angle-of-attack. Robotic force measurements confirmed that this downwards rowing in air provides vertical aerodynamic force exceeding body weight at least twofold. To direct the upstroke wing motion into a downwards rowing stroke, the insects used a combination of body pitch and roll that often resulted in the insects flying upside-down. This atypical flight posture emphasizes the adjustments required from tiny insects to convert a flight apparatus that was originally intended for utilizing lift into a drag-utilizing propulsion system, enabling flight at low Reynolds numbers.

papers.title: Wild juvenile Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus) show seasonal acclimatization of cardiac and whole-animal heat tolerance
papers.abstract: Arctic fishes experience extreme seasonality, yet how seasonal acclimatization shapes their ability to cope with thermal variation remains poorly understood. The Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus) is one Arctic fish of immense cultural, subsistence, and economic value and encounters temperatures ranging from below 0{degrees}C to above 21{degrees}C. Thermal physiology commonly varies across life stages, but has been largely unexamined in wild juvenile Arctic char. We performed winter and summer field-based assessments of wild juvenile Arctic char thermal habitat use, whole-animal and cardiac heat tolerance, and mechanisms shaping the acute thermal sensitivity of heart rate ([f]H). Average body temperature increased from 1.2{degrees}C in winter to 8.9{degrees}C in summer, and critical thermal maximum (CTmax) increased correspondingly from 21.4 to 25.9{degrees}C. We assessed the intrinsic and maximum [f]H ([f]Hint and [f]Hmax) of anaesthetized fish during acute warming using cholinergic blockade (atropine) and either {beta}-adrenergic blockade (sotalol; [f]Hint) or stimulation (isoproterenol; [f]Hmax). [f]H increased with acute warming in both seasons and treatments. However, in summer, [f]H was more responsive to warming (Q10 from 5 to 15{degrees}C: 2.4 vs. 2.0 in winter), reached a higher peak, and continued to increase while maintaining rhythmicity up to higher temperatures, with the onset of heat-induced cardiac arrhythmia (Tarr) occurring at 23.6{degrees}C vs. 18.7{degrees}C in winter. Contrary to expectations, {beta}-adrenergic blockade had little effect on these cardiac parameters. During acute warming, winter-acclimatized fish exhibited slower atrioventricular conduction (longer PR interval) and slower ventricular depolarization (longer QRS duration), which may underlie their lower cardiac heat tolerance and the reduced responsiveness of [f]H to warming. Combined, our results show that wild Arctic char exhibit strong seasonal plasticity of acute thermal performance, demonstrating the value of field-based physiological assessments and the need to consider plasticity in evaluating responses to environmental change.

papers.title: Sex-linked genomic variation reveals reproductive skew and male-biased dispersal in polygynous sea lions
papers.abstract: Sex-biased dispersal and the resulting asymmetry in gene flow are important factors in evolution. However, their quantification in natural populations remains challenging, not least because sex-specific reproductive skew, as reflected in the mating system, further influences the relative contributions of males and females to the genetic pool of subsequent generations. Incorporating information from mitochondria (MT) and sex chromosomes (X, Y) alongside the more commonly used autosomal markers (AUT) provides a promising framework to partly disentangle confounding processes. Here, we exemplify this approach in two closely related, polygynous species with observational evidence for male-biased dispersal, the Galapagos sea lion (GSL) and the Steller sea lion (SSL). Using whole-genome resequencing data, we leveraged genetic variation among all four genomic compartments, representing genetic variation with female-only (MT), mixed (X, AUT) and male-only (Y) inheritance, to obtain information on the mating system and test for sex-specific migration across geographic and environmental boundaries. For GSL, genomic signatures were consistent with mild polygyny and a moderately elevated rate of male migration, particularly across habitat boundaries. In SSL, male reproductive skew was substantially greater, and male-biased migration was more pronounced and less habitat-dependent. Our results align with the species' life history and support a link between mating system and dispersal, but were also impacted by confounding biological processes and bioinformatic choices. This study highlights the value and challenges of population genomic approaches integrating multiple genomic compartments to infer variation in individual behaviours.

papers.title: Impact of iron-enriched diets on the nutritional composition and microbiome diversity of house crickets (Acheta domesticus)
papers.abstract: Iron deficiency (ID) and iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA) pose significant global health challenges. ID and IDA are particularly widespread in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asian countries, where reliance on plant-based foods is high. Edible insects provide an alternative nutritious food source, rich in both protein and essential minerals and trace elements. Little is known about how dietary iron manipulation affects the trace element bioaccumulation and microbiome community composition of edible insects. This study examined the impact of dietary iron supplementation on the growth, survival, nutrient profile, and microbiome of Acheta domesticus. Experimental diets were formulated using iron (II) sulphate heptahydrate, resulting in final iron concentrations ranging from 333.45 mg Fe/kg (control diet) to 6923.39 mg Fe/kg (100 mM Fe diet). Iron supplementation significantly altered the cricket trace element profile, with iron levels increasing fivefold from basal 21.38 mg/kg to 118.34 mg/kg in the highest iron treatment group. Concurrently, manganese levels showed a strong negative correlation with dietary iron, while zinc and cadmium displayed non-significant downward trends. High-iron diets statistically altered dry matter, chitin, and TBARS, whereas carbohydrates, protein, glycogen, and lipids remained stable. Amino acid profiles shifted progressively, with branched-chain, sulphur-containing, and aromatic amino acids peaking in the 25 mM Fe group. In contrast, the diversity and overall structure of the microbial community remained unaffected across all treatments. In conclusion, tailoring dietary iron can significantly boost the iron content of Acheta domesticus without compromising host survival or altering core microbial structures. To optimize insect rearing strategies aimed at alleviating human micronutrient deficiencies, a feeding dose of 10-25 mmol Fe/kg is recommended.

papers.title: Tardigrades survive reversible dormancy during spaceflight: In-orbit revival, post-flight recovery, and transcriptomic responses
papers.abstract: Long-duration space missions face substantial challenges, including limited resources and prolonged exposure to microgravity and radiation. Transporting organisms in a dormant state and reviving them at their destination could help overcome some of these limitations. However, the feasibility of this strategy has not been experimentally demonstrated in multicellular animals beyond Earth. Here, we investigated this possibility using tardigrades, microscopic invertebrates capable of entering a reversible state of dormancy. We demonstrate that dormant tardigrades can withstand near-absolute-zero temperatures (~12 mK), near-vacuum conditions (10-9 mbar), high doses of ionizing radiation (3000 Gy), and complete desiccation. We transported dormant tardigrades to the International Space Station (ISS). They were revived aboard the ISS, subsequently returned to a dormant state, and successfully revived again following their return to Earth. Approximately 45% of the space-flown tardigrades survived the 64-day experimental period. This included two dormancy-revival cycles, 18 days aboard the ISS, and prolonged periods without food or water. Importantly, surviving tardigrades retained their reproductive capacity. Transcriptomic analysis of ISS-exposed tardigrades revealed upregulation of genes associated with protein folding and stress responses, accompanied by downregulation of genes involved in energy metabolism and protein synthesis, providing insights into their molecular responses to the spaceflight environment. Together, these findings demonstrate the successful revival and re-induction of dormancy in a multicellular animal beyond Earth and establish an experimental foundation for exploring dormancy-based strategies for future long-duration space missions.

papers.title: A baseline for aquatic parasite diversity in West African mangroves: host-parasite records, DNA barcodes, and an experimental design for future use
papers.abstract: Macroparasites represent a major fraction of biodiversity and biomass in marine ecosystems, yet remain substantially underrepresented in ecological surveys and food-web models, particularly in the Global South. This study addresses this geographic bias by providing the first comprehensive ecological survey of macroparasite communities of fishes in a West African Marine Protected Area (MPA) and adjacent Open-Access Area (OAA) characterised by mangrove forests. We collected 5,020 parasite specimens from 10 fish and one crab species in the Saloum Delta, Senegal, identifying 27 parasite species across all major taxa. Our findings include 15 new records for Senegal of which 11 are also new for West Africa. Additionally, 64% of host-parasite combinations constitute new host records. We provide 208 DNA barcodes, offering the first molecular data for 31% of these species globally and establishing a reference library for future DNA metabarcoding efforts in the region. Using sample size-corrected biodiversity indices and mixed-model analyses, we detected significant variations in parasite infracommunities and component communities between the MPA and OAA, demonstrating the feasibility of using comparative study designs to monitor fisheries impacts on parasite diversity in the Saloum Delta. Furthermore, the identification of trophically transmitted parasites provided evidence of unstudied food-web connections, e.g. predator-prey linkages between fishes and higher-trophic-level definitive hosts including birds and elasmobranchs. By integrating morphological identification, molecular data, and archiving of voucher specimens into publicly accessible, curated collections, this study establishes a new baseline for marine parasite biodiversity in West Africa and provides a methodological blueprint for surveying understudied regions.

papers.title: Suitability of clove oil for the euthanasia of four ornamental fish species: Goldfish (Carassius auratus), Bristlenose catfish (Ancistrus sp.), Midas cichlid (Amphilophus citrinellus) and Three-spot gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus)
papers.abstract: Euthanasia of ornamental fish is usually performed by immersion in an anaesthetic bath. However, it may be difficult for private fish owners to access anaesthetics, and alternative methods are limited. Clove oil is commonly available in drugstores and its use for fish euthanasia has been reported. However, there is a lack of scientific literature supporting its suitability for this purpose and of available species-specific protocols. Our study aimed to assess the suitability of clove oil to euthanise goldfish (Carassius auratus), bristlenose catfish (Ancistrus sp.), Midas cichlid (Amphilophus citrinellus) and three-spot gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus). Time to loss of reflexes and to cessation of opercular movements were recorded. Aversive reactions and histological gill lesions were compared with positive and negative controls, and reversibility of euthanasia attempts was assessed. Opercular movements did not reliably cease in goldfish, even under high clove oil concentrations (1000 mg/L). Clove oil caused loss of indicators in Midas cichlid at a concentration of 1000 mg/L, and in bristlenose catfish and three-spot gourami at a concentration of 400 mg/L. Five Midas cichlid recovered after treatment with clove oil. Clove oil caused severe gill lesions to goldfish and Midas cichlids. The results show that clove oil is not suitable for humane euthanasia of goldfish and Midas cichlid. Additionally, some studies have questioned the ability of clove oil to induce loss of consciousness in fish. Therefore, we recommend avoiding euthanasia with clove oil when suitable alternatives are available and using a secondary killing method, as euthanasia attempts are not always irreversible.

papers.title: A novel methodology for assessing reinforcement choice in primates under human care
papers.abstract: Positive Reinforcement Training is a technique commonly employed in zoological collections to elicit a desired behaviour from an animal under human care. Typically, a food item is offered as a reward for performing that behaviour. Three non-human primate species (Mandrillus sphinx, Pan troglodytes, and Hylobates lar) were offered four different foods (banana, grape, apple, and sweet potato) in a series of choice experiments. Latent variable models were employed to investigate which foods were the best selection to use as reinforcement items. Results show that food preference varies between the three primate species. Pan troglodytes and H. lar showed strong preferences for grape and banana, whereas M. sphinx showed a very strong preference for sweet potato. This study indicates that foraging ecology might play an important part in fruit selection and preference in primates. The findings highlight that understanding a species' natural behaviour and dietary preferences is key to informing reinforcement and training decisions.

papers.title: Sea slugs unplugged: Review of subpopulation sampling in phylogeographic studies of nudibranchs and their allies
papers.abstract: Nudibranchs and other sea slugs include many cryptic species groups with unknown phenotypic and ecological diversity. How broadly and deeply should researchers sample those cryptic species pairs to capture the genetic variation within each species and potential adaptive differences between species? Fast and inexpensive surveys of genetic diversity that sample a single well-known locus across the geographical range ("phylogeography unplugged") have long been used to identify structured populations and guide choice of sampling localities for subsequent comparative genomic or phenotypic studies of the same species. Results from such studies might also be used to better understand the expected relationships between sampling and population structure in future comparative studies in other species (including many marine gastropods) for which an unplugged phylogeographic survey is not available or impractical. We reviewed analyses of molecular variance that used mitochondrial barcode sequences from marine sea slugs, and we asked whether there are characteristic patterns of subpopulation sampling that are associated with the magnitude and geographical scale of differentiation. We found wide variation in sampling designs: studies with both many and few samples discovered significant population differentiation or broadly similar distribution of haplotypes on both large and small spatial scales, in species from different higher taxonomic groups and oceans. We found two significant associations between sampling variables and population genetic variables, and we suggest using those associations to help guide (or understand the consequences of) sampling design in future studies.

papers.title: A comprehensive identification protocol for postcranial bones of Southeast Asian Ruminantia. Part 2: Morphological criteria for small and medium-sized species
papers.abstract: The taxonomic identification of postcranial elements from small and medium-sized ruminants represents a significant challenge in zooarchaeological and Late Quaternary paleontological studies, particularly in biodiversity-rich regions such as continental Southeast Asia. This study presents a comprehensive osteological reference framework for the small and medium-sized Ruminantia of this region, based on a comparative sample of 228 specimens representing 14 species across three families (Bovidae, Cervidae, and Moschidae). Osteological characters were first described on a small initial specimen set and subsequently scored across the full sample. Although a small number of character states were found to be unique to specific taxa, most proved highly variable, limiting their individual identification potential. To address this, a Random Forest and a Naive Bayes classifier were applied to assess the discriminatory power of character combinations across four taxonomic ranks (Family, Subfamily, Genus, and Species) on independent bones. Both approaches performed similarly, achieving mean identification accuracies of 87-86% at the family level, 69% at the subfamily level, 50% at the genus level, and 35-33% at the species level. The Naive Bayes models were further deployed as an interactive web application, allowing users to perform bone identification based on any combination of observable character states from a single anatomical element. Our results highlight the limits of morphological identification of postcranial elements in this taxonomic and biogeographic context, while demonstrating that a transparent, reproducible, and statistically grounded approach can still represent a significant step forward for zooarchaeological and Late Quaternary paleontological studies in Southeast Asia and beyond.

papers.title: A comprehensive identification protocol for postcranial bones of Southeast Asian Ruminantia. Part 3: Morphological criteria for large-sized species
papers.abstract: Postcranial remains of large-bodied ruminants are abundant in the Late Quaternary record of continental Southeast Asia, yet their taxonomic attribution remains one of the least resolved problems in the zooarchaeology of this biodiversity-rich region. We address it here with an osteological identification protocol covering the six large ruminant species of the mainland: Bubalus bubalis, Bos javanicus, Bos sauveli, Bos gaurus, Budorcas taxicolor and Rusa unicolor, built from a comparative sample of 109 skeletons. A total of 148 discrete characters over 27 skeletal elements representing 442 states were defined on a restricted set of individuals, then scored across the entire sample. Most proved remarkably stable within taxa with 80.0% of the character/taxon combinations showing a dominant state at a frequency above 95%, and a substantial number of states occurred in a single family, subfamily, genus or species. Character combinations for taxonomic identification were then evaluated by the use of two supervised machine learning methods, a random forest model and a naive Bayes classifier at each of four taxonomic ranks. The two behaved almost identically, with mean accuracies of 95-94% for families, 93% for subfamilies, 89% for genera and 76% for species; only the three closely related and unevenly sampled species of Bos resisted consistent separation. The weighted naive Bayes models are distributed as a standalone web application in which any combination of states observed on a single element returns attribution probabilities for every rank. Together these results offer a transparent and statistically explicit alternative to expert judgement for the identification of Late Quaternary postcranial mammal remains, in Southeast Asia and elsewhere.

papers.title: A common marking method influences fish-parasite interactions
papers.abstract: Being able to identify the same individual organism through time is essential to robustly address many outstanding questions in ecology and evolution. For organisms that can move, and that have no reliable identifying features, researchers must often use some form of artificial marking system. In fish, a commonly used system is Visible Implant Elastomer (VIE) marking. Previous studies indicate that this marking system does not alter the survival, growth, or behaviour of marked fish. Here, using 26 VIE-marked and 46 control guppies, Poecilia reticulata, I found that VIE marking indeed did not impact fish growth. However, one month after marking, VIE-marked fish experienced an estimated ~3.7-fold higher Gyrodactylus turnbulli parasite burden during experimental infections. Two months post-marking, G. turnbulli individuals transmitted faster to VIE-marked than unmarked fish, although at this timepoint their subsequent growth was not different on fish from different treatment groups. Despite its lack of impact on common metrics of fish health, therefore, VIE marking appears to have important, long-lasting impacts on fish-parasite interactions. These findings suggest caution with assuming that marking animals is biologically neutral: that assumption may fail when the response variable involves host-parasite interactions.

papers.title: Note on a Small Chlamyphoridae (Xenarthra, Cingulata) from the Amazon, Brazil
papers.abstract: The Awa-Guaja are one of the last hunter-gatherer peoples in the world and live in Indigenous reserves in northwestern Maranhao, Brazil. The Guaja Ethnographic Collection consists of animal remains found during excavations of the community s refuse areas, conducted between 1987 and 1990. This study presents a taxonomic reassessment of a small Cingulata specimen from this collection. The specimen, previously identified as Euphractus sexcinctus, consists of a complete right femur whose taxonomic identity was reevaluated through comparative morphological and metric analyses using specimens from scientific collections and data from the specialized literature. The results revealed that the femur is smaller than those observed in individuals of E. sexcinctus and exhibits a combination of anatomical features resembling those found in the genera Chaetophractus, Cabassous, and Euphractus. Despite these similarities, the observed morphological differences do not allow a reliable identification at the genus level. Therefore, the specimen was provisionally assigned to the family Chlamyphoridae, and its identification was retained at the family level.

papers.title: Identification of insecticidal double-stranded RNAs targeting the proteasome pathway in the hop flea beetle Psylliodes attenuata using dsRIP
papers.abstract: The hop flea beetle, Psylliodes attenuata, is a major pest of hop (Humulus lupulus), an important crop for the brewing industry. Restrictions on chemical insecticides and insecticide resistance create a need for alternative control strategies. RNA interference (RNAi) uses double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to silence essential pest genes and cause insecticidal effects. In this study, we aimed to establish P. attenuata as an RNAi-based pest control target. We generated a transcriptome assembly using a public RNA sequencing dataset and used the dsRIP web platform to identify essential gene targets and design effective dsRNAs. Three dsRNAs targeting proteasome subunits were tested in feeding bioassays by applying them to hop leaf disks. The treatments caused significant mortality of up to 64% and feeding inhibition of up to 45%. Sequencing of small RNAs bound to the RNA-induced silencing complex identified predominantly 21-nucleotide small interfering RNAs produced from the orally delivered dsRNAs, supporting activation of the RNAi pathway. Additional RNA sequencing of adults enabled assembly of a higher-quality transcriptome with 89% BUSCO completeness for future RNAi studies. Overall, the feeding bioassays and molecular resources establish P. attenuata as a promising target for RNAi-based pest control and demonstrate the usefulness of dsRIP for RNAi research in insects previously unstudied at the molecular level.

papers.title: An integrated semantic publishing workflow for taxonomy: a review of the Afrotropical dung beetle genus Amietina (Coleoptera: Scarabaeinae)
papers.abstract: Taxonomic studies generate large amount of descriptive information, yet species treatments are usually written directly as natural-language text. This approach makes the underlying phenotypic information difficult to extract, reuse computationally, and maintain consistently across studies. We present an integrated workflow connecting Phenoscript, GitHub, and Overleaf. Species descriptions are written semantically in Phenoscript using biological ontologies, making their phenotypic content computable and reusable; they are then stored and version-controlled in GitHub and synchronized with an Overleaf manuscript, where human-readable descriptions are rendered directly for publication. The workflow reduces repetitive copying and formatting, preserves revision history, and promotes the production of FAIR phenotypic and taxonomic data. We apply this workflow to the African dung beetle genus Amietina Cambefort, 1981 (Coleoptera: Scarabaeinae: Onthophagini), and describe four new species from Tanzania---A. bondarevi n. sp., A. grebennikovi n. sp., A. mazumbaiensis n. sp., and A. praedicta n. sp.---bringing the total number of recognized species to eight. We also provide new distributional records, present an updated identification key, and discuss microendemism in Amietina across the Eastern Arc Mountains.

papers.title: A pilot computer-vision model trained to identify slide-mounted scale insect pests from the family Rhizoecidae
papers.abstract: The emerging field of image classification using computer vision has yet to address a rather challenging group of insect pests--soft-bodied insects that are preserved on microscope slides. This includes many notoriously invasive herbivores that have a significant impact on agriculture, such as members of the hemipteran suborder Sternorrhyncha. Using root mealybugs (Hemiptera: Rhizoecidae) as a test case, we gathered high-resolution extended depth of field images from museum specimens and trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to identify and distinguish among 16 root mealybug species that are encountered as agricultural pests in plant quarantine or greenhouses. A pretrained EfficientNetV2-M model was trained using BioEncoder. Our dataset contained 1,607 images, with 41 to 239 images per category. Performance was improved through the adoption of augmentation techniques. Upon completion of training, the model achieved macro precision, recall, and F1 scores of 80.1%, 79.3%, and 79.1%, respectively. The model demonstrated classification metrics >= 80% for seven species. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to visualize the morphological features associated with the test-image classification. Grad-CAM images highlighted meaningful diagnostic features to distinguish among species rather than focusing on uninformative visual artifacts or specimen damage, demonstrating the models utility for identification purposes. The results suggest that further development of the model should incorporate at least 200 training images per species with a minimum resolution of 600x600 pixels. The model was designed to be adaptable; images can be added to improve its performance, and more species can be incorporated as specimens become available, expanding on the taxonomic breadth of its application. Computer-vision identification tools have the potential to enhance rapid response capabilities in plant quarantine at ports-of-entry in the United States and globally.

papers.title: Shared landscapes, shared risk: Echinococcus multilocularis infection in coyotes is linked to agricultural land and altered green space in a major U.S. metropolitan area
papers.abstract: Alveolar echinococcosis (AE), caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, is among the most lethal zoonotic helminthic diseases affecting humans. Historically rare in North America, human and canine AE cases have risen sharply over the past decade, coinciding with the spread of a more virulent European-type haplotype and the emergence of coyotes (Canis latrans) as a principal definitive host in and around urban centers. Despite growing recognition of E. multilocularis as an emerging public health concern, the host- and landscape-level factors that concentrate infection risk within urban environments remain poorly understood. We used monitoring data from the Chicago metropolitan area to assess E. multilocularis prevalence and test demographic and land cover predictors of infection among urban coyotes. Fecal samples from 85 coyotes were screened via real-time PCR, and land cover association with E. multilocularis infection within individual home ranges or capture-based buffers was investigated using generalized linear models. Overall, 27.1% of coyotes were infected. Infection status was unrelated to age or sex, but coyotes with a greater proportion of agricultural land or altered open land cover, such as golf courses, cemeteries, and manicured parks, within their home ranges had significantly higher odds of infection (ORagriculture = 2.84; ORaltered open spaces = 2.07). These landscapes are also heavily used by people and domestic pets, suggesting elevated potential for zoonotic spillover in human-dominated areas rather than natural or forested habitat. Our findings identify specific, human-accessible landscapes that sustain E. multilocularis transmission in a major U.S. metropolitan area and provide a framework for prioritizing surveillance, targeted anthelmintic intervention, and public health outreach in expanding urban coyote populations across North America.

papers.title: Antenna cells of ascidian larvae are gravity-sensing neurons
papers.abstract: Ascidians are the closest living relatives of vertebrates, and they share a basic body plan including the dorsal central nervous system. The central nervous system of ascidian tadpole larvae controls their swimming behavior. In particular, for the first few hours after hatching, larvae swim upward. Gravity is sensed by an organ called the otolith, which resides in a brain vesicle. Although this sensory information is thought to be transmitted to two antenna cells abutting the otolith, direct evidence that the antenna cells function as gravity-sensory neurons has been lacking. In the present study, we first identified a regulatory element of the Vglut gene that drives expression in antenna cells and otolith-associated ciliated cells. Using this upstream regulatory element, we specifically overexpressed the apoptosis-inducing gene, Bax, in antenna cells and otolith-associated ciliated cells, and succeeded in their targeted ablation. These Bax-overexpressing larvae lost their preference for upward swimming. Because antenna cells have axons and otolith-associated ciliated cells lack neurites, our observation indicates that antenna cells are the sensory neurons for gravity. In addition, our experimental method for targeted disruption of cells using an enhancer element and Bax provides a valuable tool to examine neural circuit functions at cellular resolution.

papers.title: Pufferfish inflation: drivers of axial and hoop skin strain and regional variation across the body
papers.abstract: Pufferfish skin undergoes large multi-axial extensions during defensive inflation behaviour, as water is pumped into the stomach and the fish increases its body volume threefold. This remarkable capacity for deformation thus raises questions on how skin extension is spatially distributed across the body, and how skin extension relates to changes in body volume and stomach pressure. However, directly measuring skin extension remains experimentally challenging, particularly when attempting to preserve the body's complex 3D geometry and natural multiaxial strain during ex vivo testing. We used biplanar x-ray videography to measure skin strain (fluoromicrometry) and body volume (dynamic digital endocast) simultaneously with stomach pressure recordings during natural and artificial inflations in porcupinefish (Diodon holocanthus). We found no significant difference in maximum body volumes, body dimensions, peak pressures, and skin extension at maximum inflation between natural and artificial inflation conditions. In all inflations, volume increased steadily while stomach pressure only increased during the last 25-50% of inflation. Skin extension varied biaxially, with mean strains reaching up to 74% in the axial direction and 112% in the hoop direction as the fish became nearly spherical. The greatest skin extensions occurred most dorsocranially (axial) and ventrolaterally (hoop). Strains in the hoop direction were only significantly different between body regions (dorsal, lateral and ventral), with the greatest hoop strains occurring in the ventral body region. Our findings may provide insight into existing hypotheses regarding the relationship between volume, pressure, and skin structure and behaviour, while also providing direct in vivo measurements to inform biomimetic design.

papers.title: An update on the mosquito fauna of Aguascalientes, Mexico: morphological and molecular identifications, host-feeding patterns, and the removal of Aedes idahoensis (Theobald) from Mexico
papers.abstract: To better understand taxonomic identity and feeding patterns of mosquitoes in all physiographic regions and sub-regions of Aguascalientes, Mexico, we conducted surveillance followed by morphologic analysis and DNA metabarcoding. We targeted the Sierra Madre Occidental, Central Plateau, and Neo-Volcanic Axis. We sampled natural larval habitat for immature stages and adults were collected using Shannon and CDC light traps, mechanical aspirators, and human landing catch method. In addition, curated specimens from Aguascalientes deposited in a local institution were re-examined. Overall, 5,227 mosquito specimens consisting of 357 larvae, 199 larval exuviae, 373 pupal exuviae, 33 pupae, 3,000 females, 1,264 males, and 1 male genitalia were examined using taxonomic keys. Most immature and adult species (n = 20/34 species representing 58.8% coverage) were barcoded for molecular species designation, and a subsample (n = 64) of engorged female mosquitoes were analyzed for blood feeding patterns. Two subfamilies, four tribes, seven genera, 14 subgenera, and 34 species were identified, which one tribe, three genera, nine subgenera, and 22 species are new records. Phylogenetic analysis of specimens from Aguascalientes identified 20 species. Morphological observation of mosquitoes deposited in entomological collections resulted in the removal of Aedesidahoensis from Mexico, leaving the country with a total of 255 species documented. Bloodmeal metabarcoding was successful in 23 mosquitoes of five species, revealing evidence of feeding on more than a single vertebrate species in 17 individuals. Birds were the most common host with the cattle egret (Ardea ibis) found in 18 out of 23 mosquitoes. This update on the taxonomic identity and mosquito richness and feeding patterns from Aguascalientes affords a better understanding of the ecology of medically important mosquito species.

papers.title: What happens when Arctic sea-ice melts? Macroalgae as a summer refuge for sympagic nematode Theristus melnikovi
papers.abstract: Sea ice-associated (sympagic) nematodes are particularly vulnerable to ongoing Arctic sea-ice loss, yet the capacity of these sympagic species to persist in ice-free habitats remains poorly understood. We investigated the summer habitat and taxonomic identity of the sympagic nematode Theristus melnikovi, in Svalbard, using an integrative taxonomic approach. We barcoded 17 morphologically identified nematodes from macroalgae (5), sea-ice (9), and sediment (3). Morphological analysis and phylogenetic reconstruction based on 18S rRNA gene analyses revealed that the macroalgae-associated T. melnikovi represented a habitat-associated phenotypic variation of T. melnikovi rather than a morphotype of the benthic nematode T. acer. Macroalgae-associated specimens were generally shorter and stouter, with proportionally longer tails and shorter anterior structures than their ice-associated counterparts, resulting in a superficial resemblance to T. acer. Despite these morphological differences, molecular analyses consistently placed macroalgae-associated individuals within the T. melnikovi clade and haplotype. Our results highlight that T. melnikovi may have a greater ecological flexibility than previously assumed and macroalgae may offer an alternative (summer) habitat, or refuge, during ice-free periods. This capacity could become increasingly important as Arctic sea-ice duration and extent continue to decline.

papers.title: Repeated coastal observations and molecular confirmation of Alatina grandis (Cubozoa: Alatinidae) in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea
papers.abstract: Cubozoans are rarely documented in the Red Sea, and the taxonomic identity of large alatinid medusae previously reported from the Gulf of Aqaba has remained uncertain. Historical observations from Eilat in 1997 and 2000 were reported as Carybdea alata, although their exceptionally large size was recognized as being within the range of C. grandis (currently Alatina grandis); unresolved carybdeid taxonomy at the time prevented a definitive species-level assignment. Following more than two decades without documented observations, five large alatinid medusae were recorded on separate occasions along the Eilat coastline between July 2025 and August 2026. One specimen was collected, while high-resolution in situ photographs and video recordings of live medusae provided material for morphological assessment. Diagnostic morphological characters were consistent with Alatina grandis, and molecular analysis of the collected specimen independently confirmed its identity as A. grandis. These findings provide the first molecular confirmation of A. grandis from the Gulf of Aqaba and the Red Sea and establish the identity of the alatinid medusae documented during the recent series of observations. The clustering of five observations within one year, following more than two decades without documented occurrences, raises questions regarding the temporal occurrence and distribution of this rarely reported cubozoan in the northern Red Sea.

papers.title: Shifts in the Maternal Gut Microbiome Across Pregnancy are Associated with Energetic Status in Phayre's Leaf Monkeys
papers.abstract: During pregnancy, mothers experience physiological changes that support fetal development, including shifts in energy utilization and increasing insulin resistance during late gestation. While these changes benefit the fetus, they can also impose energetic costs that affect the mother's physical condition and metabolic phenotype. Previous studies suggest that the gut microbiome, a key regulator of female metabolism and energy harvest, may play a critical role in mediating these physiological challenges. In this study, metagenomic sequencing of the gut microbiome of 120 samples revealed dramatic shifts in gut bacterial composition and function associated with pregnancy and lactation in 14 wild Phayre's leaf monkeys, Trachypithecus phayrei crepusculus, from two groups at the Phu Khieo Wildlife Sanctuary, Thailand. Alpha diversity, beta diversity, and taxonomic composition all differed between cycling and the 3rd trimester. Furthermore, bacterial dissimilarity between these states was negatively correlated with postpartum physical condition; that is, mothers whose gut microbiota remained more stable during pregnancy recovered sooner after giving birth. Functional profiling revealed a depletion of pathways involved in purine salvage and glutamate degradation during the 3rd trimester. Overall, our study demonstrates that the gut microbiome undergoes substantial changes during pregnancy, and the stability of these microbial communities predicts postpartum maternal health and potentially influence lifetime reproductive output.

papers.title: Relatedness and last male sperm precedence in Cheilomenes sexmaculata: Implications for inbreeding avoidance
papers.abstract: Avoidance to mate with relatives is a common evolutionary strategy, as it helps maintain genetic diversity and overall fitness within populations. Females often prefer unrelated males to mitigate the risks associated with inbreeding, such as the expression of deleterious recessive alleles. This preference can involve various post-copulatory mechanisms through which females bias paternity towards males with potentially better genes. The phenomenon of last male sperm precedence, where the last male to mate with a female tends to sire the majority of offspring, is well-documented in ladybird beetles. However, how relatedness affects this phenomenon remains unclear. This study aims to investigate whether paternity share is altered when the last male to mate with a female is related to her. By conducting double mating experiments with two different morphs (typical and intermediate) as phenotypic markers, we seek to determine if relatedness disrupts last male sperm precedence. It was hypothesised that females of Cheilomenes sexmaculata will prefer unrelated males over related ones, irrespective of mating order, potentially breaking down the last male sperm precedence. This preference for unrelated males was reflected in our results with unrelated males exhibiting enhanced reproductive success. Females were more fecund and exhibited higher egg viability with unrelated males. Greater paternity share was observed for unrelated males when the second male was related to the female. This study highlights the dynamic nature of sperm precedence and the role of mate quality in female mate choice, emphasizing the importance of inbreeding avoidance in sexual selection.

papers.title: Dipteran wing damage discriminates between flight motor inertial-elastic distributions
papers.abstract: Insects frequently experience irreversible wing damage, yet many maintain flight by adjusting their wingbeat. In Diptera, wingbeat frequency generally increases as wing inertia is lost, but considerably less than predicted by classical models of the flight motor. In this work, we use an inverse-problem approach to identify passive mechanical features of the dipteran flight motor that explain this discrepancy and reproduce experimentally-observed frequency scaling. Combining spatially resolved reconstruction of wing inertia and motor elasticity, finite-element analysis of thoracic deformation, and data-driven viscoelastic models of asynchronous flight muscle, we identify that a compounding interaction between wing root flexion, wing aerodynamics, and muscular viscoelasticity explain the depressed scaling of wingbeat frequency with loss of inertia. Wing inertia is strongly non-uniform and dominated by the vein structure, leading to further depression with respect to loss of area. But, by contrast, thoracic effective inertia is negligible across a wide array of Dipterans and does not contribute to damage-related scaling. Together these results indicate that much of the dipteran flight motor's responses to wing damage can emerge passively from interactions between the wing, thorax, and muscles; and suggest that a hybrid-elastic architecture with a compliant wing root may be widespread across Diptera. More broadly, we identify wing damage as a tool that can quantitatively discriminate between different candidate models of the insect flight motor, and suggest that altered motor operating conditions can identify mechanical properties difficult to infer from intact flight alone.

papers.title: Long-term storage of Hermetia illucens (Diptera: Stratiomyidae) larvae
papers.abstract: The production of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL), Hermetia illucens (L. 1758) (Diptera: Stratiomyidae), for organic waste conversion and sustainable biomass production is gaining increasing interest. Maintaining sufficient larval stocks is essential for continuous production, yet practical methods for long-term storage remain limited. This study evaluated the effects of temperature (15{degrees}C and 27{degrees}C), larval density, and substrate coverage on BSFL survival and growth over a 12-week storage period. Storage conditions significantly affected substrate moisture, larval survival, and development. Covering the substrate with hydrated straw pellets and aluminium foil reduced water loss and minimised maintenance requirements. The highest survival rate, approximately 70% after two months of storage, was obtained at 15{degrees}C using this combination of hydrated straw pellets and aluminium foil. Following storage, larvae showed high survival and pupal hatching rates under standard rearing conditions, indicating that prolonged storage did not compromise larval fitness. These results demonstrate that storage at 15{degrees}C with hydrated straw pellets and an aluminium cover provides a practical, low-maintenance strategy for maintaining reserve BSFL stocks and ensuring a stable supply of larvae for production and research purposes.

papers.title: Larval thermal tolerances and future dispersal potential of the subtropical-to-temperate sea urchin Tripneustes australiae
papers.abstract: The distribution and dispersal of marine ectotherms is mediated by their thermal tolerances, and as the oceans warm species distributions are shifting. Developmental thermal tolerances of marine invertebrates with a pelagic life-history phase can be used to predict the potential for local extinctions and range extensions. In southeast Australia, Tripneustes australiae is an ecologically important sea urchin species as it undergoes periodic outbreaks and can transform ecosystems through intense herbivory. We investigated the embryonic and early larval developmental tolerances of T. australiae with respect to its current distribution, to predict current and future dispersal capacity. The optimal thermal window for survival, normal development and developmental progression of T. australiae ranged between 17 and 23{degrees}C, with probability of survival at these temperatures remaining above 85% throughout the experiment. This developmental thermal window overlaps with the current thermal regime experienced across the adult distribution. This suggests that T. australiae may have a similar thermal window in its adult and early larval life history stages. Further, T. australiae may have the potential to persist at its warm-range edge into the future and to disperse and range shift poleward in coming decades. Indeed, we show that the temperature at which larvae have a 50% probability of survival may extend poleward across the Bass Strait by 2100. The persistence of T. australiae in its mid-range, its potential to disperse poleward, and increased grazing pressure from periodic outbreaks, may impact temperate macroalgal habitats already at risk from warming and concentrated grazing by other sea urchin taxa.
